articles.title: France faces sole fish crisis as Channel stocks collapse
articles.text:
France faces sole fish crisis as Channel stocks collapse
Advertisement
Environment
France faces sole fish crisis as Channel stocks collapse
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 28 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 28 Nov 2026 11:44 CET
Add a comment
This photograph shows sole on a stall at an open-air market in Caen, northwestern France on November 27, 2026. (Photo by Guillaume SALIGOT / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
Huguette Germain's seafood restaurant is close to the Normandy D-Day beaches and a short walk to a monument to lost sailors, but Germain and the region's fisherman are increasingly worried about a new battle: disappearing sole.
Sole meunière, the emblematic flat fish cooked in lashings of butter, is a staple delicacy of any French fish restaurant worth its salt. But stocks in the eastern Channel separating France and Britain have mysteriously collapsed, sending shock waves through dining rooms and trawler fleets.
"It's become very difficult to find, and there's a good chance we'll have to take it off the menu next year," said Germain, who runs La Trinquette in the fishing village of Grandcamp-Maisy.
Sole meunière has been a staple at her establishment since the 1980s. "But there is no longer enough to be found in Normandy, so we're bringing it in from Brittany" -- at increasingly prohibitive prices.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
"Even mackerel is becoming hard to come by," Germain added. "Moving forward, we'll inevitably have to cut back on these types of fish."
With the 2027 quotas on sole fishing slashed in a bid to save stocks, many French fishermen in the region fear they will be put out of business.
The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) -- a senior scientific authority -- has recommended a catch limit of 163 tonnes in the eastern Channel, stretching from the Belgian border to the Gulf of Saint-Malo. This is 87 percent down on 2025.
"It's heartbreaking," said Dimitri Rogoff, president of the Normandy Fisheries Committee. "Sole is what has put food on my table for 30 years. I never thought I'd see this in my lifetime."
He called the crisis "a complete failure in resource management."
Over-fished
"It is going to be a catastrophe," predicted Quentin Yonnet, 45, who has a trawler in Port-en-Bessin.
Advertisement
"In the spring, the boats will be left tied up at the dock, and some will end up for sale. It's as simple as that."
Yonnet said some 150 boats in the Seine Bay on the Normandy coast depend on the sole that is shared with trawlers from Britain and Belgium.
Channel sole has long been over-fished. In the early 2000s, the trawlers caught up to 5,000 tonnes a year in the eastern Channel.
A customer buys fish at an open-air market in Caen, northwestern France on November 27, 2026. (Photo by Guillaume SALIGOT / AFP)
Since 2015 "we have seen a continuous reduction in fishing, yet the stock is not recovering," said Raphaël Girardin, a fisheries scientist at France's main sea institute IFREMER. The sole that survive are also getting smaller and the reasons are mainly unknown.
"We haven't identified a specific culprit," said Girardin, though he did pinpoint some "environmental factors."
In winter, sole spawn hundreds of thousands of eggs offshore. After hatching, the larvae drift for two months. As young sole, they spend the first two years in coastal mudflats that serve as nurseries. Even minor environmental changes can have a radical impact.
Over the past two centuries, Seine Bay has lost a third of the intertidal mudflats that were a vital habitat for juvenile sole. Much has been dredged away so bigger vessels can enter the key river Seine.
Advertisement
Olivier Le Pape, a researcher in fisheries ecology at L'Institut Agro, said that if the bay was in the same conditions as the 19th century there would already be 20 percent more fish.
But Le Pape, who has studied a similar phenomenon in the Bay of Biscay down the coast, said the decline appears to begin as early as the larvae stage though he cannot say why.
Plankton may be changing or their may be problems with the timing of the larvae hatching and the plankton blooms. Le Pape said that could be more fallout from global warming.

articles.title: Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
articles.text:
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
Presented By Talent Berlin
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
There's far more to Berlin than its UNESCO-protected club culture. For those seeking an exciting career move, the German capital offers a heady mix of both business and pleasure.
Published: Thu 29 Oct 2026 15:45 CEST
Photo: Talent Berlin
For some, living and working abroad is a lifelong dream. It’s choosing where to start this new life that’s the million-dollar question. A city might offer great job opportunities but fall short on other things that make life outside work fulfilling—or vice versa.
In Berlin, you don't have to choose. As one of Europe's capitals for innovation and start-ups, it combines career opportunities with a rich cultural scene, more to do outside of work than one could manage in a lifetime, and a diverse international community ( around 25 per cent of Berliners are foreign-born).
It’s a city that’s famous for its tolerance and readiness to embrace different lifestyles. After all, Berliners aren't born—they're made at the Bürgeramt.
A city buzzing with ideas
Berlin's reputation as a start-up capital isn't just hype. In 2026, StartupBlink named it the EU's "Best Community-Driven Ecosystem". Its venture-backed start-ups are worth €169 billion and support some 94,000 jobs.
The Talent Berlin LinkedIn page posts Jobs of the Week, as well as other useful information about what's happening in Berlin's talent and innovation ecosystem.
Explore the Berlin-Brandenburg start-up ecosystem
While Berlin is home to one of Europe's leading start-up hubs, its business landscape is as varied as it is prolific. It has a booming tech sector, world-class life sciences and biotech communities, a growing green economy, and, famously, a thriving creative scene.
The city practically pulses with ideas and innovation; it's an incredibly exciting place to be for those working in science and research, biotechnology, and energy and environment, as well as other industries that will play a vital role in the decades to come.
Many of Berlin's innovations emerge where these industries intersect, from sustainable fashion and food science to digital health and the creative use of AI.
International professionals working in the city often cite its cross-sector ecosystem as one of its greatest advantages. Once you have your foot in the door, you can hop between start-ups, established companies, research, and emerging industries.
Photo: Talent Berlin
You won't get lost in translation
Learning a new language is all part of the fun of moving abroad, and German is, naturally, widely spoken in Berlin.
However, in those early days — or even years — of acclimatisation, you can easily get by in English, though it doesn't hurt to have a German-speaking friend who can help with certain administrative tasks.
Taking the time to learn German doesn't just expand your career options and make bureaucracy easier; it helps you integrate into Germany itself, not just Berlin's international community.
Keep up with Berlin’s start-up scene
If you’re serious about settling in Berlin for the long term, an integration or language course gives you essential German skills and practical knowledge of German society to help you live and work independently.
The city that never sleeps
In Berlin, when the 9-to-5 ends, the 5-to-9 begins.
Whatever you like to do in your spare time, whether you're into climbing, clubbing, or quite literally anything in between, you'll find it in Berlin.
The city’s tree-lined streets are crammed with cafes, bars, restaurants, and indie stores. Parks punctuate the city, and you're rarely more than a short journey from a wild swimming lake, forest, or nature reserve where you can enjoy the great outdoors.
Photo: Paula Schmidt / Pexels
Many Berliners forgo a car for a bike; the city is easy to cycle, and an extensive, affordable public transport system makes getting around without a car relatively straightforward.
The elephant in the room
Berlin is an attractive place to live, so its housing market is stretched—to put it lightly. That makes it tough to find somewhere to live, especially for newcomers.
Somewhat counterintuitively, you generally need to be in Berlin while searching for an apartment, so you can view the property and meet the landlord or estate agent before signing.
Many people start with temporary accommodation while they familiarise themselves with the rental process and look for a long-term contract.
Check with your employer about any relocation or housing assistance they may offer, and take a look at Talent Berlin's housing guide as a starting point. The organisation also offers a housing service your employer may already use, so it’s worth asking about this before you make the move.
Could Berlin be your next move?
Berlin has its quirks — some that make life easier, others that can make it more challenging. But for skilled professionals, few cities offer the same combination of career opportunity, innovation, internationalism, and life beyond work.
You may move to Berlin for the job, but it won't be the only reason you stay.

articles.title: Inside France: €1 homes, hidden trains and egg mayonnaise
articles.text:
Inside France: €1 homes, hidden trains and egg mayonnaise
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: €1 homes, hidden trains and egg mayonnaise
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 28 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 28 Nov 2026 10:40 CET
Add a comment
A chef competing in the egg mayonnaise world championships in Saint-Ouen on November 23, 2026. Photo by JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the latest '€1 homes' scheme - actually this one is almost-free land - aimed at addressing population loss in rural France to the Eggs Mayonnaise World Championship, and the surprise reason for the Eurostar strike, here's the latest news and talking points from France.
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.
Another week, another '€1 homes' story from rural France - the latest is actually slightly different, the mairie is offering almost-free plots of land for people to build their own home.
But all these schemes - and most of them have quite a few conditions, so they're not quite as good as they sound - are about the same thing; tackling a shrinking and ageing population.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
The problem is most acute in rural France, where individual mayors are running these sort of schemes to try and lure people back to their villages, but it's part of a wider trend across France, and indeed across most of the western world.
READ ALSO: Where can I find France's €1 homes?
A report from the French national statistics agency this week projects that by 2070 there will be 3.2 million fewer people in France. More importantly, it projects that one third of the population will be aged 65 or over, with obvious consequences for the pension system, the economy, public services and the workplace.
It's worth noting that these projections assume current migration trends continue, but almost half of the candidates in the 2027 election have pledged to severely reduce migration - thereby cutting off the supply of new working-age people at the same time as the French birthrate declines.
READ ALSO: MAPS: Where in France will have the oldest population by 2070
Advertisement
This is not a problem unique to France, and across the Western world we have seen various incentive schemes and tax breaks all fail to solve the issue of falling birthrates, not that it has stopped them from trying - for example, Edouard Philippe proposes a three-year income tax holiday for new parents.
But sooner or later politicians across Europe are going to face the fact that they only have three options;
Solve the social problems that people say make them delay having children (housing shortages, low wages, fears about climate change)
Tell the population that they're going to have to accept much higher pension contributions or a longer working life, along with a reduction in public services
Convince voters that actually immigration is a good thing
Sooner or later? My money is on later.
Advertisement
Talking France
We discuss the latest from the French presidential elections in the new episode of the Talking France podcast, along with the police shooting law that has been dubbed a 'licence to kill' and the strange history of 'trouser permits for women' in France. Listen here.
Band of (mayonnaise) brothers
This week in France saw the Egg Mayonnaise World Championships - and to give you an idea about how passionate people can be about this dish, at least two of the people there had egg mayo-related tattoos (one of the competing chefs had œuf on one leg and mayonnaise on the other, while one of the judges has '8 minutes, 40 seconds' tattooed on his wrist - the precise boiling time for a perfect egg, apparently).
And the Association pour la sauvegarde l’œuf mayo, which organised the contest, is just one of the hundreds of confréries (brotherhoods) dedicated to the protection of French dishes or food products.
Thinking of all those people dedicating their lives to protecting and promoting things like Quiche Lorraine, Roscoff onions or cassoulet gives me a warm glow - truly, is there a better use of one's time upon this earth?
Advertisement
Language victory
And one of the greatest moments in any French learner's life is when they get to contradict or correct an actual French person - this happened to me this week, when I knew that a certain phrase was also an idiom and she did not.
I thought about getting a tattoo to immortalise this glorious moment, but settled for a French Word of the Day instead.
READ ALSO: French Expression of the Day: Un train peut en cacher un autre
Vive la France
A surprise strike caused major disruption on the Eurostar this week and, while I have every sympathy for anyone whose journey was disrupted, I couldn't help but laugh when I learned the spark for the strike.
The company had held a lavish leaving party in a five-star hotel in London for the outgoing CEO, while telling unions involved in pay negotiations that there was no money for pay raises. The staff at Gare du Nord got wind of this, and immediately walked out.

articles.title: French expression of the day: Au bout
articles.text:
French expression of the day: Au bout
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French expression of the day: Au bout
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 27 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 28 Nov 2026 09:40 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
This expression is key if you want to master the art of French exasperation.
Why do I need to know au bout?
Because dramatic flair is pretty important in France - and in the French language.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
Au bout or à bout, pronounced oh-boo (listen here), translates to 'at the end', 'on the verge' or 'on the edge'.
This is a slang expression and it's usually accompanied by de ma vie - au bout de ma vie means 'at the end of my life'.
Not to be used literally, this means that you are exhausted and tired, maybe even a little sick of the world.
For example, if you have had a long week and you're swamped with work even though it's Friday afternoon and you're practically dying to go home and put your feet up, you could exclaim:
Je suis au bout de ma vie ! - I am at the end of my life!
Really, it means 'I'm exhausted' or 'I can't take it anymore'.
For a serious conversation about someone who really is at the end of their life, say having palliative treatment for cancer, you would say fin de vie - end of life.
Advertisement
Use it like this
It's usually thrown out in exasperation, and it's a good expression to use slightly ironically. No one will think you're actually dying, but it will definitely earn you sympathy points.
A good alternative to au bout de ma vie is au bout du rouleau, which means 'exhausted' or 'burnt out'.
You can also shorten it to simply, je suis à bout and linger on the boooouuuuuut (however, this is slang).
Or, for extra melodrama, say, je suis au bout du bout du bout de ma vie - I'm at the end of the end of the end.
READ ALSO: The 10 best French expressions for the everyday exasperation of life
You can also use it on others:
Les pauvres, l'équipe était complètement au bout de sa vie à la fin du match. - Poor team, they were totally knackered at the end of the game.
Elle est au bout de sa vie en ce moment, elle taffe trop. - She's completely drained right now, she's working too much.
Advertisement
Synonyms
Je n'en peux plus - I can't take (it) anymore
J'en ai marre - I'm sick of this
Je suis épuisé - I'm exhausted
Je n'ai pas le moral - I'm not motivated anymore
Don't mistake it for this..
Au bout can also mean 'all the way', as in J'y vais jusqu'au bout ! - I'm going all the way!
Here, au bout reflects a set goal rather than a personal state of mind.
For example, before a football game the captain might shout:
On y va jusqu'au bout les gars ! - We're going to go all the way lads!
On continue jusqu'au bout de la rue ? - Shall we continue all the way to the end of the road?

Emma Albright - emma.albright@thelocal.com
Published: 23 Nov, 2026 CET.
Add a comment
Which parts of Germany have the hardest tap water? (Photo by ANNE-CHRISTINE POUJOULAT / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
Limescale can be a familiar household nuisance, and it can do more than leave chalky deposits on your taps as it can also dry out your skin and hair. But tap water levels of hardness vary significantly across France.
If you live in France, you may have noticed a white residue building up around your taps, shower-heads and kettles. This is usually caused by calcaire (limescale), a common feature of French tap water.
Water that has high levels of minerals, and therefore where limescale builds up quickly, is usually colloquially known as 'hard' water. In addition to the effect on your kettle, you'll likely notice that it's more difficult to lather up soap.
But not all water is equally hard, and it varies considerably around France.
Water hardness is measured in French degrees (°f) - not to be confused with Fahrenheit - using a scale known as titre hydrotimétrique (TH). It is calculated by measuring the concentrations of calcium and magnesium in a sample of tap water and converting them into an equivalent concentration of calcium carbonate.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
One French degree corresponds to 10 milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre of water. The higher the figure, the more minerals the water contains, and therefore the harder it is.
Hardest water
According to an analysis of official water-quality monitoring data from France's regional health agencies (ARS), the Nord département (Hauts-de-France) has the hardest tap water in mainland France, with a median hardness of 36.4°f.
The Hauts-de-France region includes five départements that feature among the six hardest in the country.
Parts of Normandy, particularly the Eure, Calvados and Seine-Maritime départements, also have relatively hard water. Further east, several départements in the Grand Est region, including the Marne, Ardennes and Haute-Marne, record relatively high levels.
Advertisement
Charente-Maritime and Vienne, in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, are among the départements with the highest median readings. See the map here.
Paris
Parisians are no strangers to limescale either. Paris has a median water hardness of 26.3 °f, placing it in the moderately hard category. However, the surrounding départements vary considerably.
Seine-Saint-Denis has a median of 27.7 °f, while Seine-et-Marne reaches 27.5 °f. The Val-d'Oise records 26.7 °f, compared with 24.1 °f in the Hauts-de-Seine and 19.5 °f in the Yvelines.
This means that two people living just a few kilometres apart in the Paris region can experience noticeably different levels of limescale in their homes.
Where is the softest water?
Parts of central and south-western France have considerably softer water.
The Lozère département, in Occitanie, has the softest water in mainland France, with a median hardness of just 1.6 °f. Other départements with particularly soft water include: Cantal (Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes): 3.2 °f, Haute-Loire (Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes): 6.3 °f and Corrèze (Nouvelle-Aquitaine): 7.6 °f.
The contrast is largely explained by geology. Water passing through limestone-rich rocks tends to absorb more calcium and magnesium, making it harder. In areas with granite and other less soluble rocks, water generally contains fewer dissolved minerals.
This helps explain why parts of the Massif Central have particularly soft water, while the chalk and limestone landscapes of northern France tend to produce harder water.
Advertisement
Water hardness map of France, going from red - the hardest - to blue. (Source: Water Hardness Map by LIMPEO)
The map above is a screenshot of an interactive map showing water hardness across France, down to the individual municipality. It uses official drinking-water quality data from the French Ministry of Health.
The tool allows households to check how hard their tap water is, see where it falls on the scale from soft to very hard, and understand how limescale can affect pipes and household appliances such as water heaters, washing machines and kettles.
Blue shows soft water, green is in between, orange is hard water, and red is very hard water.
The French Ministry of Health also provides an online tool allowing residents to check the official water-quality results for their municipality, based on monitoring carried out by regional health agencies.
You can also check the Robinet Clair website, which allows you to see the water hardness across France.
Is hard water safe to drink?
Some people don't like the taste, but hard water is not considered a health risk. Calcium and magnesium are minerals naturally found in drinking water, and their presence does not make tap water unsafe to consume.
The main inconvenience is limescale accumulation, which can build up inside kettles, coffee machines, washing machines, boilers and pipes. It can also leave white marks on bathroom glassware and build up in your shower head.
You might also find that your skin or hair become dry after a prolonged period in an area with hard water.
Advertisement
READ ALSO: Six things to know about tap water in France
Can you reduce water hardness at home?
If you live in an area with particularly hard water, there are several ways to limit limescale build-up in your home. The most effective solution is to install a water softener (adoucisseur d'eau), which removes calcium and magnesium from the water. These systems are usually installed where the water enters the property and can help protect household appliances, pipes and boilers.

articles.title: French far-left leader demands 'overhaul' of German ties
articles.text:
French far-left leader demands 'overhaul' of German ties
Advertisement
Politics
French far-left leader demands 'overhaul' of German ties
AFP - news@thelocal.com
Published: 28 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 28 Nov 2026 04:26 CET
Add a comment
French hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of The France Unbowed (LFI) party, takes his seat as people applaud during an event to present his book "Now, the People! Revolution in the Twenty-First Century" that was translated into German, at the Babylon Berlin cinema in Berlin, Germany, on November 27, 2026. (Photo by Tobias SCHWARZ / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
French hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon on Friday called for an "overhaul" of ties with Berlin, voicing stinging criticism of Germany's economic dominance in the EU and its record on military spending.
The France Unbowed (LFI) party leader, who is polling in second place for April's election, told French broadcaster LCI during a Berlin visit that he sees a "need for a thorough overhaul of the French-German relationship".
"I am hostile to the liberal (economic) policy of German governments that dominates the European Union," the 75-year-old said ahead of the launch of the German edition of his latest book at Berlin's Babylon cinema.
Mélenchon's economic platform, which includes a proposal to cancel French debt held by the European Central Bank, is dramatically opposed to traditional German doctrines of tight budgets and low borrowing.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Mélenchon -- currently the favourite to reach a run-off against far-right veteran Marine Le Pen -- has also railed against Chancellor Friedrich Merz's commitment to transform the German military into the "strongest conventional army in Europe".
"We have the duty to ask: to make war against whom?" he said Friday, warning that Paris could be drawn into unwanted conflict as Germany's growing military strength makes it a "target" for other countries.
Mélenchon's rivals have accused him of cosying up to President Vladimir Putin's Russia, with LFI's pledge to leave NATO a particular concern for many of France's allies amid the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The far-left party leader has been highly critical of Germany's position in the conflict, accusing Merz's government of sabre-rattling.
"They need to tone it down, because all this one-upmanship leads nowhere," he said.
Advertisement
At the book launch, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine was not mentioned directly, but Mélenchon said he would "immediately" begin discussions with China in the event of his victory in the election.
"We do not want war with China and we will not help the Americans to make war against the Chinese," he said.
Earlier, Mélenchon flatly denied charges he is "Germanophobic", calling himself a "sort of disciple of Karl Marx" and a lover of Beethoven.
He also expressed pride at the German translation of his latest book, published in English under the title: "Now, the People! Revolution in the 21st Century."
The politician further touted his close ties with Germany's far-left Die Linke party, which finished first in Berlin's state election in September.
Mélenchon met the party's national leader Ines Schwerdtner on Friday, saying the two were "united in mobilising against an economy of rearmament and war".

articles.title: OPINION: Yes, even legally-resident foreigners in France should fear a Le Pen win
articles.text:
OPINION: Yes, even legally-resident foreigners in France should fear a Le Pen win
Advertisement
Politics
OPINION: Yes, even legally-resident foreigners in France should fear a Le Pen win
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 24 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Tue 24 Nov 2026 16:15 CET
7 comments
Marine Le Pen answering questions at a pre-election debate. Photo by Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
'It won't affect people who are here legally,' is a phrase foreigners in France might hear if the conversation turns to the chances Marine Le Pen becoming French president next year. It's a comforting thought, but people who say this are wrong, writes Emma Pearson.
With a crucial presidential election looming, conversations about politics are becoming even more fraught in France, and with her commanding leading in the polls it's very hard to have one without mentioning Marine Le Pen.
And this is where foreigners in France are faced with phrases like 'Yes, but she's only after the illegals, legally-resident foreigners will be fine' or 'Yes, but this doesn't really affect you, you already have your residency permit' or 'Yes, but she won't actually be able to do the stuff in her manifesto, she'll be limited by the parliament/constitution'.
Usually these types of comments are well meaning, trying to offer comfort or reassurance to people who might be worried about what 2027 will bring.
But whatever the intention, they're dangerously misguided.
The policies
Marine Le Pen has not published her full manifesto for 2027 yet, but she has given several keynote speeches outlining her policies, and laid out parts of her programme in an alternative budget.
While there is indeed a focus on clamping down on illegal migration, there are also plans to severely restrict new migration to France with changes to the visa and carte de séjour system.
Advertisement
But even for those already in France with a residency permit - even those who already have a long-term residency permit - there are policies that could potentially have a big impact on their lives.
READ ALSO: What would a Le Pen presidency mean for foreigners in France?
Chief among these is her policy of 'French preference', which she announced in her very first campaign speech - this doesn't merely give preference to people who have French citizenship, it excludes completely non-French people from a series of important areas in life including social housing and benefits, and certain types of work.
It's crucial to note that 'French preference' affects anyone who doesn't have French citizenship - including those who have the passport of an EU country and are therefore not required to get a residency permit to live in France.
Then there's her tax proposal - she wants to add an extra tax of €1,000 per year, per employee for any company that employs non-EU citizens, thereby making them much less attractive to employers.
And if you lose your job because of this, you'd better find another one soon - her other policy is that a carte de séjour should not be renewed for anyone who has been out of work for 12 months or more (her deputy Jordan Bardella says six months or more, clearly the details are still being worked out).
Don't miss our editor's weekly breakdown of the 2027 French presidential election race
Those who have French citizenship have a lot less to worry about, but her party has in the past proposed restrictions on dual nationals, including barring access to certain jobs.
The guardrails
But would she actually be able to do any of this?
It depends on the policy, and also what happens with parliament - whether a newly-elected president would call fresh parliamentary elections, and whether they manage to get a majority in parliament.
A fractured and divided parliament like the current one would be able to block legislation - although it's worth noting that the centre-right and centrist candidates have similar policies on things like tightening up rules on cartes de séjour, visas and French citizenship.
READ ALSO: Compared - The French presidential candidates' policies for foreigners in France
However the constitution of the Fifth Republic gives significant powers to the president at the expense of parliament, with constitutional tools like Article 49.3 and Article 47 allowing presidents to pass laws without the support of parliament, albeit within certain limits.
Advertisement
Many of her policies would fall foul of the Constitutional Court because they contradict the basic principle of égalité that is enshrined within the constitution - however the constitution can be amended via the mechanism of a referendum, something that Le Pen has already said that she intends to call on the subject of immigration.
Finally, any limits on the rights of EU citizens in France would fall foul of the European Union's principle of freedom of movement - at which point we would see exactly how willing and able the EU is to take on the government of one of its founder members and the 'joint engine' of the EU project.
Likewise, anything that affects the rights of Brits in France who moved prior to 2021 risks being a breach of the Withdrawal Agreement. But again, this would depend on the EU being prepared to take action against France on behalf of those British residents, at a time when it may have much larger problems on its hands.
Unintended consequences
When people say that Le Pen is not targeting groups such as British retirees or American tech workers, that's probably true.
However, legislation can have unintended consequences - for example, former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau probably wasn't targeting British or American retirees with his 2025 citizenship memo, but the changes to the rules that he outlined for French citizenship nonetheless effectively made it impossible for people who had retired to France to become French ( until the recent reversal).
